crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Earnings Call Tone
children.blurb: Earnings call tone is the sentiment, certainty, and emotional register that management and analysts convey during quarterly earnings calls, especially in prepared remarks and the question and answer session.

children.name: Supply Chain Disruption in Text
children.blurb: Supply chain disruption in text is the practice of reading written and spoken material for early signs that goods, parts, or raw materials will not move as planned.

children.name: Retail Investor Sentiment
children.blurb: Retail investor sentiment is the aggregate mood, confidence, and risk appetite of individual investors, as distinct from institutional positioning.

children.name: Event-Driven Trading
children.blurb: Event-driven trading is the practice of taking positions around discrete corporate or regulatory events, such as earnings releases, merger announcements, index changes, and court rulings.

children.name: Reading Regulatory Filings
children.blurb: Reading regulatory filings is the practice of pulling useful signals from the documents public companies and funds must file with regulators.

sections.body: Reading the Market's Language is the part of The AI Economist that treats text as market data. Earnings calls, supplier updates, forum posts, regulatory filings and news wires all carry signals that used to be read by analysts one document at a time. Language models now scan these sources at volume, scoring tone, flagging unusual phrasing and linking a sentence in a filing to a price move in a related instrument. The work is mostly classification and extraction rather than prediction, turning unstructured prose into structured features that feed screens, alerts and research notes. This site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, which gives those text signals something concrete to be compared against.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Tone scoring is reasonably mature, and most large vendors and research shops can produce a sentiment number per call or per paragraph. What remains unsolved is the gap between a measured tone shift and a tradeable outcome, because the same words can mean different things across sectors and cycles. Supply chain signals are harder, since disruption often shows up first in small supplier filings or shipping notices that are noisy and inconsistently formatted. Retail sentiment is plentiful but easily gamed, and models trained on it can mistake coordinated noise for genuine shifts in positioning. Filing analysis sits closest to solved for extraction, yet interpretation still needs a human who knows the company, and none of this work is advice or a recommendation to buy or sell anything.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages here form a chain from the spoken word to the formal record. Earnings Call Tone covers the prepared remarks and question sessions where management sets expectations, and it is the natural starting point for anyone new to text based signals. Supply Chain Disruption in Text moves outward to the suppliers, logistics notices and trade press that often react before the headline company does. Retail Investor Sentiment looks at the crowd side, the forums and social posts that can move small caps and meme names, and it pairs well with Event-Driven Trading, which handles the scheduled and unscheduled moments such as results, deals and index changes that force prices to reprice quickly. Reading Regulatory Filings closes the loop with the slowest but most authoritative source, the documents companies must file, and it connects to the site's 394 merger and acquisition filings and 150 active AI lawsuits for readers who want to see how formal disclosures are being parsed at scale.
